name: Thanumalayan Temple
story:
The Thanumalayan Temple is the soul of Suchindram, a temple town on the road between Nagercoil and Kanyakumari. It is one of the very few temples in India where the Hindu trinity is worshipped as one: the deity Sthanumalaya fuses Sthanu (Shiva), Mal (Vishnu) and Ayan (Brahma) in a single linga in the sanctum. The soaring seven-tiered white gopuram, about 40 metres tall and dense with painted sculpture, announces the temple from miles away; most of what you see today took shape in the 17th century.

Legend says the god Indra was cleansed of a curse here - suchi means purification - so a shrine of Indra Vinayaka still honours that story. Do not miss the 22-foot Hanuman, carved from a single granite block and said to have been hidden during Tipu Sultan's invasions, then reinstalled in 1930. In the Alankara mandapam, four musical pillars cut from one stone ring with different notes when tapped.

Come in the Tamil month of Margazhi (December-January) for the ten-day chariot festival, when the great temple car is hauled through the streets ringing the shrine, or arrive at dawn to hear the first hymns echo off centuries-old stone.

name: Suchindram
story:
Suchindram is a small temple town in Kanyakumari district, about 11 kilometres from Nagercoil and roughly the same from Kanyakumari at the land's end. Its name tells its story: suchi means purification, and tradition holds that Indra, king of the gods, was cleansed of sin here after the curse linked to the sage Gautama and his wife Ahalya - an episode that ties the town to the Ramayana cycle of tales.

Life in Suchindram still revolves around its great Thanumalayan Temple and the agraharam streets that frame it. Visit early, when flower sellers and oil lamps animate the stone corridors, and linger for a free lunch-hour atmosphere that bigger pilgrimage towns have lost. The twice-yearly car festivals, especially in Margazhi (December-January), turn the whole town into a single procession.

name: Meenakshi Amman Temple
story:
Meenakshi Amman Temple is the beating heart of Madurai, one of the oldest continuously lived-in cities in India. The goddess Meenakshi, a fish-eyed warrior princess born to a Pandya king, rules here alongside her consort Sundareswarar, a form of Shiva. Though the shrine is ancient, the spectacular complex you see now - 14 gateway towers covered in thousands of vividly painted gods - was largely raised by the Nayak rulers in the 16th and 17th centuries.

Look for the thousand-pillared hall with its sculpted columns, the golden lotus tank where devotees once tested the worth of Tamil poetry, and the tallest gopuram rising about 52 metres over the southern gate. In April-May the Chithirai festival restages the celestial wedding of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar, and the whole city turns out as wedding guests.

name: Brihadeeswara Temple
story:
A thousand years ago the Chola emperor Raja Raja I raised this temple to Shiva, and it still stuns first-time visitors with its scale. Completed around 1010 CE, its central vimana towers about 66 metres high, capped by a single granite block estimated at some 80 tonnes - how it was lifted remains an engineer's puzzle. The great Nandi bull facing the sanctum is carved from one stone, and Chola-era frescoes still cling to the inner walls.

Brihadeeswara is the centrepiece of the UNESCO-listed Great Living Chola Temples, and living is the right word: worship continues daily as it has for a millennium. Come at dusk, when the granite turns honey-coloured and the circumambulatory fills with locals doing evening pradakshinam.

name: Ramanathaswamy Temple
story:
On an island reached by the Pamban bridge, Ramanathaswamy is one of the twelve Jyotirlingas and one of Hinduism's Char Dham pilgrimage sites. The Ramayana tells that Rama, returning from Lanka, worshipped Shiva here to atone for killing Ravana - a Brahmin - and the linga Rama is said to have installed remains the holiest object in the temple.

The temple is equally famous for its architecture: its outer corridors, lined with more than a thousand carved pillars, are reckoned the longest temple corridors in the world, a seeming infinity of stone. Pilgrims bathe at the 22 theertham wells inside the complex and at Agni Theertham on the beach before darshan. Even non-pilgrims find the rhythm of ritual here unforgettable.

name: Kanyakumari
story:
Kanyakumari is the land's end of mainland India, where the Bay of Bengal, the Indian Ocean and the Arabian Sea are said to meet. The town is named for Kanya Kumari, the virgin goddess whose seaside temple, the Kumari Amman shrine, has drawn pilgrims for centuries; legend says she waited here for a divine marriage that never happened.

This is the one place in India where you can watch both sunrise and sunset over water on the same day, and on full-moon evenings you can see the sun set and the moon rise almost together. Walk the ghats at dawn, watch pilgrims take a dip at the Triveni Sangam, and ferry out to the rock memorials offshore for the full sweep of the cape.

name: Vivekananda Rock Memorial
story:
A short ferry ride off the tip of India stands a rocky islet where, in December 1892, Swami Vivekananda swam out and meditated for three days before his famous journey to the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago. He later said that on this rock he found clarity about his life's mission.

The memorial, inaugurated in 1970 and built by public subscription, blends architectural styles from across India, symbolising the unity Vivekananda preached. Inside, a meditation hall preserves the rock's natural footprint-like mark, revered as the goddess's footprint long before Vivekananda's time. Go in the morning before the queues, and sit quietly - the wind and the meeting seas do half the meditating for you.

name: Thiruvalluvar Statue
story:
On a small island beside the Vivekananda Rock stands a colossal stone figure of Thiruvalluvar, the Tamil poet-philosopher who gave the world the Tirukkural - 1,330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love that Tamils call their universal scripture. Unveiled on the first day of the year 2000, the statue rises 133 feet, one foot for each chapter of the Kural, atop a 38-foot pedestal representing the 38 chapters on virtue.

The combined height of 41 metres makes it one of India's great modern monuments, all the more striking for standing alone against three seas. Ferries usually stop at both rocks; climb the pedestal for the best view back to the mainland's end.

name: Shore Temple
story:
Standing against the surf of the Bay of Bengal, the Shore Temple is one of the oldest structural stone temples in South India, built by the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II around 700-728 CE. Its twin shrines to Shiva, with a reclining Vishnu between them, have watched sailors come home for thirteen centuries; fishermen once called this coast the land of the Seven Pagodas, and legend says sister temples lie drowned offshore.

The temple is part of the UNESCO-listed monuments of Mamallapuram, where Pallava sculptors first translated wood-and-brick architecture into granite. Visit at sunrise when the stones glow, and notice how wind and salt have softened the carvings - time itself is the ongoing sculptor here. The temple withstood the 2004 tsunami that briefly exposed more of the old port.

name: Pancha Rathas
story:
The Pancha Rathas are five shrines each carved from a single granite boulder in the 7th century, experiments by Pallava masons in shaping whole temples out of living rock. Though named for the five Pandava brothers and Draupadi of the Mahabharata, they were never actually consecrated - which is why you can walk freely through them today.

Each ratha copies a different architectural style, from a simple hut-roofed shrine to a full temple tower, like a stone catalogue of early South Indian design. Look for the life-sized elephant and lion carved alongside, and the unfinished details that show exactly how the sculptors worked from the top of the boulder downward.

name: Kapaleeshwarar Temple
story:
In Mylapore, Chennai's oldest quarter, the Kapaleeshwarar Temple honours Shiva and his consort Karpagambal, the goddess of the wish-yielding tree. Legend holds that Parvati once worshipped Shiva here in the form of a peacock - mayil in Tamil - which is how Mylapore got its name. The original seaside shrine was demolished by the Portuguese in the 16th century, and the present temple was rebuilt inland; its colourful gopuram is around three centuries old.

The streets around the temple tank form one of Chennai's most atmospheric walks, especially at dusk when lamps and jasmine sellers appear. If you visit during the Panguni festival in March-April, you will see Mylapore transform into a ten-day street celebration of gods, music and food.

name: Fort St. George
story:
Fort St. George is where the British story in India began in earnest: the English East India Company raised this fortress in 1639-1644, and the settlement that grew around it became Madras, modern Chennai. It was the company's first stronghold in India and the seed of its empire.

Inside the walls, St. Mary's Church, consecrated in 1680, is the oldest Anglican church in India, and the Fort Museum displays weapons, coins and documents from the East India Company era, including early colonial-era artefacts. The complex still houses the Tamil Nadu legislative assembly and secretariat, so it remains a working seat of power nearly four centuries on - one of the oldest continuously used fortifications in the country.

name: Rock Fort
story:
Trichy's Rock Fort is a massive outcrop of ancient rock - geologists date the stone itself to over three billion years old - rising abruptly from the flat city. Temples have crowned it for well over a millennium: the Pallavas, Cholas and Nayaks all built here, and the rock later saw fierce fighting in the 18th-century Carnatic Wars between the British and French.

Climb the several hundred rock-cut steps past the Thayumanavar Shiva temple, set in a cave partway up, to the small Ucchi Pillayar Ganesha shrine at the summit. The reward is a panoramic view over the Kaveri, Srirangam island and the gopurams of the great Ranganatha temple - one of the finest city views in Tamil Nadu, best taken in the cool of early morning.

name: Jambukeswarar Temple
story:
Jambukeswarar at Thiruvanaikaval is one of the five great elemental Shiva temples of Tamil Nadu, representing water - and fittingly, the linga in the sanctum sits in a natural spring that keeps it perpetually half-submerged. Tradition credits the early Chola king Kocengannan, some 1,800 years ago, with building the shrine, making it one of the oldest living temples on the Kaveri delta.

The goddess here is Akhilandeshwari, whose shrine rivals the Shiva sanctum in importance; the noon ritual, where a priest dresses as the goddess to perform worship, is a beloved local custom. Five concentric walls and seven courtyards give the temple the feel of a fortified town of gods - wander inward slowly and watch the crowds thin into silence.

name: Nataraja Temple
story:
Chidambaram is where Shiva dances. The Nataraja Temple enshrines him as the cosmic dancer whose steps create and dissolve the universe, an image that has become the very emblem of Indian art. It is also the akasha, or ether, temple among the five elemental shrines, and it holds a famous mystery: the Chidambaram Rahasyam, a curtained space that, when revealed, shows only golden vilva leaves - God as empty space itself.

Chola kings gilded the sanctum roof, and the temple's east gopuram carves all 108 dance poses of the Bharatanatyam canon in stone. The temple is uniquely managed by hereditary Dikshitar priests. Time your visit for the Natyanjali festival around Maha Shivaratri, when dancers from across India perform before the Lord of Dance himself.

name: Adi Kumbeswarar Temple
story:
Kumbakonam, the temple town of the Kaveri delta, takes its very name from this shrine. Legend says that when the great flood dissolved the world, Shiva broke the kumbha - the pot holding the nectar of creation - and it came to rest here; the linga of Adi Kumbeswarar is said to be made from that sacred pot's earth.

The temple's tall eastern gopuram and long corridors anchor the old town, but the deeper rhythm is the Mahamaham festival, held once every twelve years when hundreds of thousands of pilgrims bathe in the great Mahamaham tank nearby, believing all of India's holy rivers meet in its waters. Even on an ordinary evening, Kumbakonam rewards slow wandering - bronze-casters, filter coffee and a dozen other ancient shrines lie within walking distance.

name: Airavatesvara Temple
story:
A few kilometres from Kumbakonam at Darasuram, the Airavatesvara Temple is the third of the UNESCO-listed Great Living Chola Temples, built in the 12th century by Rajaraja Chola II. Smaller than Thanjavur's giant, it trades size for jewel-box detail: the front mandapa is conceived as a chariot drawn by horses, and miniature friezes narrate the lives of the Shaiva saints in panels the size of postcards.

Listen as you climb - a flight of steps here is famously said to ring with musical notes underfoot. The temple is named for Airavata, Indra's white elephant, who is said to have worshipped Shiva at this spot. Come in the late afternoon when the low sun picks out the carved stonework and the tour buses have gone.

name: Mysore Palace
story:
The Amba Vilas Palace was the seat of the Wodeyar maharajas, who ruled Mysore for some five centuries. When the old wooden palace burned down during a wedding in 1897, the regent Maharani commissioned English architect Henry Irwin, and the present Indo-Saracenic fantasy - domes, arches and colonnades in grey granite and pink marble - was completed in 1912.

Inside, the Durbar Hall and the Kalyana Mantapa dazzle with stained glass, cast-iron pillars from Glasgow, mosaic floors and carved doors; the golden howdah displayed at Dasara once carried the goddess Chamundeshwari on elephant-back. Visit on a Sunday night or during the Dasara festival, when the whole palace is outlined in roughly a hundred thousand light bulbs - one of India's great sights.

name: Chamundeshwari Temple
story:
Rising above Mysuru, Chamundi Hill is crowned by the temple of Chamundeshwari, the fierce goddess who slew the buffalo-demon Mahishasura - the demon who gave Mysuru its name. The Wodeyar kings adopted her as their family deity, and her gilded idol remains the focus of the city's Dasara procession each autumn.

You can drive up or climb the thousand-odd steps from the foot of the hill; partway stands a colossal Nandi bull, nearly five metres high, carved from a single granite boulder in the 17th century. From the summit, the view over the palace city and the Kaveri plain explains why kings and gods both chose this hill.

name: Virupaksha Temple
story:
Amid the ruins of Vijayanagara, one of the greatest cities of the medieval world, Virupaksha Temple still lives: worship here has continued unbroken since at least the 7th century, outlasting the empire that glorified it. The Vijayanagara kings expanded the shrine, and the nine-tiered eastern gopuram, about 50 metres high, rose under Krishnadevaraya in the early 16th century.

Inside, look for the temple elephant blessing visitors, the painted ceiling panels, and a curious pinhole-camera effect in a dark chamber that projects the gopuram upside down on the wall. Step outside onto Hemakuta hill at sunset and the boulder-strewn ruins of a fallen capital glow amber all around - few temple settings on earth match it.

name: Vittala Temple
story:
The Vittala Temple is the showpiece of Hampi, raised in the 16th century at the height of Vijayanagara's power. Before its gateway stands the Stone Chariot - a granite shrine on wheels modelled on a temple car, so iconic it appears on India's fifty-rupee note.

The Maha Mandapa astonishes with its musical pillars: slender granite columns that, when struck, were said to ring like percussion instruments, the so-called sa-re-ga-ma pillars (now protected from tapping). Walk the colonnaded bazaar street leading away from the temple, imagine it stacked with diamonds as Persian travellers described, then sit by the riverine ruins at sunset - Hampi's magic is as much in its silence as its stones.

name: Chennakeshava Temple
story:
In 1117 CE the Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana commissioned this temple to mark his victory over the Cholas, and legend says it took over a century and generations of sculptors to finish. Built of soft soapstone that hardens with age, every surface is worked like jewellery: friezes of elephants, lions, scrollwork and gods run in bands around the star-shaped base.

Inside, lathe-turned pillars gleam like polished metal, and the bracket figures - madanikas, celestial dancers frozen mid-gesture under the eaves - are among the finest sculptures in India; one shows a lady wringing water from her hair. Guides love to demonstrate the Narasimha pillar, once said to rotate on its base. Belur remains a living temple, so remove shoes and linger for the evening aarti.

name: Hoysaleswara Temple
story:
Halebidu was the Hoysala capital, and the Hoysaleswara Temple, begun around 1120 under King Vishnuvardhana, is its surviving masterpiece - a twin shrine on a star-shaped platform carrying what may be the most dense stone carving anywhere in India. Bands of elephants, lions, horses and scrolling foliage support an unbroken pageant of gods, dancers and battle scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.

The temple was never fully completed: raids by the Delhi Sultanate in the 14th century sacked the city, and Halebidu - the name means old city - never recovered its glory. That interruption froze the work of the sculptors mid-stroke. Walk the outer wall slowly, guidebook in hand; every few feet reveals another small miracle of detail.

name: Badami Cave Temples
story:
Badami was the capital of the early Chalukyas, who in the 6th century carved four magnificent cave temples straight into the red sandstone cliff above the town. Three are Hindu and one Jain, and together they are among the earliest great rock-cut monuments of the Deccan.

The first cave holds a celebrated relief of an eighteen-armed Nataraja striking eighty-one dance poses; the third, the largest, carries huge, serene panels of Vishnu in his many forms, including one dated inscription of 578 CE. After the caves, descend to the green Agastya lake flanked by the Bhutanatha temples, and climb to the fort above for a view over the gorge where an empire's sculptors learned their trade.

name: Golconda Fort
story:
Golconda began as a mud fort of the Kakatiya kings, but it was the Qutb Shahi dynasty of the 16th and 17th centuries that raised the granite citadel you see today. For generations this was the heart of the world's diamond trade - the mines of the Golconda region yielded legendary stones, and the Koh-i-Noor and the Hope diamond are both said to have passed through these markets.

Clap your hands at the Fateh Darwaza gate and, thanks to a clever acoustic design, the sound can be heard at the Bala Hisar pavilion on the summit, nearly a kilometre away - the fort's ancient warning system. Climb the 360-odd steps for sunset over Hyderabad, then stay for the evening sound-and-light show that retells the rise and Mughal conquest of the fortress.

name: Charminar
story:
In 1591 Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, founder of Hyderabad, raised the Charminar at the crossing of his new city's two great roads - by tradition, to mark the end of a devastating plague. Four graceful minarets rise about 56 metres from its grand arches, and the little mosque on the upper floor is among the oldest in the city.

The Charminar remains the beating heart of the old city: Laad Bazaar beside it glitters with lacquer bangles, Irani cafes pour sweet chai, and the lanes towards the Chowmahalla Palace reward aimless wandering. Climb to the first floor for a view over the bazaar rooftops, and come back at night when floodlights turn the monument golden above the crowds.

name: Taj Mahal
story:
In 1632 the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, grieving his beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal, ordered a tomb that would outshine all others. Some twenty thousand artisans laboured for over two decades on the Yamuna's bank, raising a mausoleum of white Makrana marble inlaid with semiprecious stones in floral pietra dura so fine it seems painted.

The Taj is a study in symmetry and illusion: the four minarets lean subtly outward so they would fall away from the tomb in an earthquake, and the calligraphy around the great arch swells in size with height so it reads evenly from the ground. Visit at dawn when the marble shifts from grey to rose to gold, and see it again by moonlight if you can - Shah Jahan's monument to love rewards every hour.

name: Agra Fort
story:
Akbar the Great began this red sandstone fortress-palace in 1565, and his grandson Shah Jahan later replaced many of its structures with the white marble pavilions you see today - the Khas Mahal, the Sheesh Mahal mirrored palace, and the graceful Diwan-i-Khas where the Peacock Throne once stood.

The fort's most poignant corner is the Musamman Burj, an octagonal marble tower where the imprisoned Shah Jahan spent his last years, held by his own son Aurangzeb, gazing across the river at the Taj Mahal where his wife - and later he himself - lay buried. Allow half a day: the fort is a walled city in itself, and every courtyard carries three generations of Mughal ambition.

name: Fatehpur Sikri
story:
In 1571 Akbar, grateful to the Sufi saint Salim Chishti who had foretold the birth of his son, built an entire new capital here - palaces, audience halls, a great mosque - and then, barely fourteen years later, abandoned it, most say for want of water. The result is a perfect ghost city of red sandstone, preserved as the Mughals left it.

Enter through the Buland Darwaza, a 54-metre victory gate raised to celebrate the conquest of Gujarat, and you reach the courtyard of the Jama Masjid and the white marble tomb of Salim Chishti, where childless couples still tie threads seeking blessings. In the palace quarter, seek out the Panch Mahal's five diminishing storeys and the carved pillar of the Diwan-i-Khas, where Akbar held his famous debates among faiths.

name: Red Fort
story:
Shah Jahan built the Red Fort between 1638 and 1648 as the palace-citadel of his new capital, Shahjahanabad, and for some two centuries the Mughal emperors ruled India from behind these red sandstone walls. Persian verses inlaid in the Diwan-i-Khas still proclaim: if there be a paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this.

The fort saw empire's splendour and its fall - Nadir Shah carried off the Peacock Throne in 1739, and the British tried the last Mughal, Bahadur Shah Zafar, here after 1857. Every Independence Day since 1947 the Prime Minister has hoisted the flag from its ramparts. Walk in through the covered bazaar of Chatta Chowk, imagine the elephants that once passed under the Naubat Khana's drums, and stay for the evening light-and-sound show.

name: Qutub Minar
story:
Victory has rarely looked like this. Qutb-ud-din Aibak, founder of the Delhi Sultanate, began the Qutub Minar around 1199 to celebrate the new Muslim rule in India, and his successor Iltutmish completed the 73-metre tower of fluted red sandstone, its bands carved with Quranic verses and intricate arabesques.

Around it lies the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, the first built in North India, assembled partly from the columns of demolished temples - the carved Hindu and Jain motifs still visible in its cloisters tell their own story of conquest and reuse. In the courtyard stands the famous Iron Pillar, over sixteen centuries old, which has resisted rust through Delhi's monsoons, a metallurgical mystery older than the sultanate itself. The whole complex is UNESCO-listed and best seen in the golden hour.

name: Humayun's Tomb
story:
When the Mughal emperor Humayun died in 1556, his widow Haji Begum commissioned a tomb unlike anything India had seen - a great domed mausoleum of red sandstone and white marble set in a charbagh, a four-part paradise garden divided by water channels. Completed around 1572 under the Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas, it was the first grand garden-tomb of the subcontinent.

A century later its lessons bore fruit at Agra: the Taj Mahal is in many ways Humayun's Tomb perfected in marble. Beyond the main mausoleum, wander to the tomb of Isa Khan and the serene avenues where Delhi-ites picnic at dusk - this UNESCO site remains one of the capital's most peaceful places, its symmetry most magical in late-afternoon light.

name: India Gate
story:
Rising 42 metres at the eastern end of Rajpath, India Gate is Edwin Lutyens's memorial to the tens of thousands of Indian soldiers who died fighting for the British Empire in the First World War and the Third Afghan War; the names of over 13,000 of them are inscribed on its arches. It was unveiled in 1931.

Beneath the arch burns the Amar Jawan Jyoti, the eternal flame added after the 1971 war to honour the Unknown Soldier. Come at dusk, when the monument glows under floodlights and the lawns fill with families, balloon sellers and ice-cream carts - a solemn war memorial that has become Delhi's favourite evening promenade.

name: Amber Fort
story:
Perched on a ridge above Maota Lake, Amber was the stronghold of the Kachhwaha Rajputs before they founded Jaipur. Raja Man Singh I began the palace-fortress in 1592, and his successors added courtyards for over a century, blending Rajput and Mughal styles in warm sandstone and marble.

The climb through Suraj Pol leads to a sequence of wonders: the Diwan-i-Aam's columned hall, the painted gateway of Ganesh Pol, and the Sheesh Mahal, whose walls glitter with thousands of tiny mirrors - a single candle once lit the whole chamber. From the ramparts you can see the Great Wall-like fortifications snaking over the hills to Jaigarh Fort. Arrive early, before the heat and the crowds, and let the lake reflection double the palace for you.

name: Hawa Mahal
story:
The Palace of Winds is Jaipur's unmistakable face: a five-storey screen of pink sandstone raised in 1799 by Sawai Pratap Singh, pierced by 953 small latticed windows. Its purpose was practical as much as pretty - the honeycomb facade let royal women observe street life and festivals below without being seen, honouring the purdah of the court.

Those same jharokhas funnel the desert breeze, giving the palace its name and its natural air-conditioning. The facade is the spectacle; the interior is a maze of ramps and small chambers worth a quick climb for the view over the bazaar and the City Palace. See it at sunrise, when the pink city earns its nickname, from a rooftop cafe opposite.

name: City Palace
story:
When Maharana Udai Singh II founded Udaipur in 1559 beside Lake Pichola, he laid the first stone of this palace; over the next four centuries his descendants of the Mewar dynasty - among the oldest royal lines in the world - built one towering balcony, courtyard and cupola after another until the palace became a small granite-and-marble city above the lake.

Inside, the museum winds through mirrored and tiled apartments, miniature painting galleries and courtyards like the Mor Chowk, where peacocks are rendered in brilliant glass mosaic. From the upper terraces the Lake Palace floats dreamlike on Pichola. Mewar's rulers styled themselves not kings but custodians of the god Eklingji - a pride you can still feel in every crest and gateway.

name: Lake Pichola
story:
Lake Pichola began in 1362, by tradition as a dam built by a grain-carrier tribesman, and was enlarged when Udai Singh founded his city on its shore. Four islands dot its waters, and on them sit two of India's most romantic buildings: the Lake Palace, Jag Niwas, raised in 1746 as a royal summer retreat and now a fabled hotel, and Jag Mandir, where Prince Khurram - the future Shah Jahan - once took refuge, and whose marble domes are said to have inspired elements of Mughal design.

Take the sunset boat from the City Palace jetty: ghats, palaces and havelis slide past in gold light, and you will understand why Udaipur is called the Venice of the East. In monsoon, when the lake fills, the city feels afloat.

name: Jaisalmer Fort
story:
Rising from the sands of the Thar on Trikuta hill, Jaisalmer Fort was founded in 1156 by Rawal Jaisal, a Bhati Rajput ruler whose desert capital commanded the caravan routes to Central Asia. Its yellow sandstone walls burn gold at sunset, earning it the name Sonar Quila, the Golden Fort.

Unlike most great forts, this one is alive: a substantial share of the old town's people still live within its walls, in havelis carved like lace from the same honeyed stone. Wander the winding lanes to the seven exquisite Jain temples of the 12th-16th centuries, climb to the cannon points for a view over the endless desert, and stay overnight inside the walls if you can - after the day-trippers leave, the fort belongs to its residents and the stars.

name: Mehrangarh Fort
story:
Mehrangarh rises 120 metres above the blue city of Jodhpur, on a cliff so sheer its walls seem to grow out of the rock. Rao Jodha founded the fort in 1459 when he moved the Rathore capital from Mandore; legend says a hermit's curse on the displaced hill was appeased only by a man volunteering to be buried alive in the foundations.

Inside the seven great gates - Jayapol still bears cannonball scars from an 1806 battle with Jaipur - lie palaces of astonishing refinement: the mirrored Sheesh Mahal, the gilded Phool Mahal, and Moti Mahal's pearl-white hall. The museum's palanquins, howdahs and miniature paintings are superb. From the ramparts, the indigo-washed old city spreads below like a sea, with the white marble cenotaph of Jaswant Thada gleaming on the ridge.

name: Gateway of India
story:
The Gateway of India was raised in basalt and yellow concrete on the Apollo Bunder waterfront to commemorate the 1911 landing of King George V, the first British monarch to visit India - though it was finished only in 1924, and the king passed a cardboard mock-up. Its Indo-Saracenic arch, blending Hindu and Muslim motifs, became the ceremonial entrance to the subcontinent for viceroys and travellers arriving by sea.

History gave the monument a final twist: in 1948 the last British troops left independent India by marching out through this very arch. Today it is Mumbai's beloved promenade - ferries leave for Elephanta Island from its steps, balloon sellers and photographers crowd the plaza, and the Taj Mahal Palace hotel watches over it all, as it has since 1903.

name: Ajanta Caves
story:
Hidden in a horseshoe bend of the Waghora river, the thirty-odd caves of Ajanta were cut by Buddhist monks in two great phases - from around the 2nd century BCE and again in the 5th-6th centuries CE under Vakataka patronage. Then the site fell silent, reclaimed by jungle, until a British officer's hunting party stumbled on it in 1819.

What makes Ajanta supreme is its painting: tempera murals that cover entire walls with Jataka tales of the Buddha's past lives, alive with courtiers, elephants, dancers and shipwrecks - ancient India's lost painting tradition surviving almost nowhere else. Caves 1, 2, 16 and 17 hold the finest panels. Carry a good torch or hire the reflector service, and give yourself a full day; this UNESCO site rewards slowness.

name: Ellora Caves
story:
Between roughly 600 and 1000 CE, three faiths carved thirty-four monasteries and temples into a two-kilometre basalt cliff at Ellora: Buddhist viharas, Hindu shrines and Jain temples, side by side in remarkable harmony. Together they form one of the largest rock-cut complexes on earth, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The climax is Cave 16, the Kailasa temple: an entire mountain-top shrine to Shiva, sculpted top-down from a single rock under the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I in the 8th century. An estimated 200,000 tonnes of basalt were removed to free the temple from the cliff, making it arguably the largest monolithic structure ever created. Stand before its towering courtyard and consider that every cornice, elephant and frieze was carved - never built - and Ellora will stay with you forever.

name: Konark Sun Temple
story:
Around 1250 CE, King Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty raised a temple to Surya the sun god in the form of his celestial chariot: twenty-four colossal carved wheels, each about three metres across, pulled by seven straining horses towards the dawn. European sailors navigating the coast called it the Black Pagoda, a landmark for ships.

The great tower over the sanctum has collapsed, but the surviving Jagamohana hall and its platform remain an encyclopaedia of Odishan sculpture - courtly life, war, music and famously frank erotic panels. The wheels are precise sundials whose spokes can still tell the time. Visit in early morning light, and if you come in December, the Konark dance festival brings the frozen dancers back to life.

name: Jagannath Temple
story:
Puri's Jagannath Temple is one of the four sacred Char Dham of Hinduism, raised in the 12th century by King Anantavarman Chodaganga of the Eastern Ganga dynasty. Its deities are unlike any others in India: Jagannath, Lord of the Universe, with his brother Balabhadra and sister Subhadra, are huge wooden figures with round painted eyes, periodically reborn in the secret Nabakalebara rite when new images are carved from sacred neem trees.

Once a year the gods leave their temple: at the Rath Yatra, three towering chariots haul them through the roaring crowds to their aunt's garden house - a festival that gave English the word juggernaut. Note that entry to the temple is restricted to Hindus; others can admire the towering spire from the Grand Road and share the astonishing mahaprasad from the temple kitchens outside.

name: Victoria Memorial
story:
When Queen Victoria died in 1901, Viceroy Lord Curzon vowed that Calcutta, capital of her Indian empire, should raise a memorial to outshine every other. The result, built between 1906 and 1921 to William Emerson's design, is a vast white wedding-cake of Makrana marble - the same stone as the Taj Mahal - crowned by a bronze Angel of Victory that, locals love to say, turns in the wind.

Today the memorial is a museum of the Raj: the Calcutta Gallery's paintings and photographs trace the city from Job Charnock to independence, and the royal galleries hold the Queen's own desk and piano. Even if you skip the museum, come at dusk when the floodlights come on and the Maidan fills with strolling families - the empire's monument now belongs entirely to Kolkata.

name: Howrah Bridge
story:
Officially named Rabindra Setu, the Howrah Bridge has carried Kolkata across the Hooghly since 1943 - a 705-metre cantilever giant of riveted steel, famously built without a single nut or bolt. Wartime urgency shaped it: steel was diverted from other projects while Japanese planes threatened the Bay of Bengal, yet the bridge rose anyway, and it has never stopped working since.

By some counts it remains the busiest cantilever bridge in the world, carrying a daily tide of buses, trucks, hand-pulled rickshaws and rivers of pedestrians between Howrah station and the city. The finest view is from a country boat at dawn, when the bridge frames the sunrise and flower-market porters stream across below; at night, floodlit, it becomes the city's glowing signature.

name: Golden Temple
story:
The Harmandir Sahib, the Abode of God, floats gold upon a sacred pool that gave Amritsar its name - the tank of nectar. Guru Ram Das founded the city and excavated the sarovar in the 16th century; Guru Arjan completed the temple in 1604 and installed the Adi Granth, Sikhism's holy scripture, within. Two centuries later Maharaja Ranjit Singh sheathed the upper storeys in gilded copper, giving the shrine its luminous skin.

Four doors open on four sides, a standing invitation to every caste and creed. Join the barefoot circuit of the parikrama, listen to the unbroken hymn-singing that fills the air, and do not miss the langar - the world's largest free community kitchen, serving simple meals to tens of thousands daily, all cooked and served by volunteers. Visit before dawn for the scripture's ceremonial awakening; it is unforgettable.

name: Jallianwala Bagh
story:
A short walk from the Golden Temple lies a garden that changed India's destiny. On 13 April 1919, during the Baisakhi festival, thousands gathered here - many simple villagers unaware of a ban on assembly. Without warning, General Reginald Dyer ordered his troops to fire on the unarmed crowd; they shot until their ammunition ran low. Hundreds died, including women and children, and many more perished leaping into a well to escape the bullets.

The massacre, and the brutalities that followed, turned a generation of moderates into freedom fighters - Tagore returned his knighthood, and the independence movement found its moral certainty. The preserved walls still bear bullet marks, the Martyrs' Well stands as it was, and an eternal flame burns at the memorial. Visit quietly; the weight of the place needs no commentary.

name: Cellular Jail
story:
On the remote Andaman Islands, the British built a prison designed for total isolation: the Cellular Jail, completed around 1906, with seven three-storey wings radiating from a central watchtower like spokes, holding hundreds of tiny cells each meant for a single prisoner. It was here that the Raj exiled the political prisoners it feared most - from the rebels of 1857 to generations of freedom fighters, including Veer Savarkar.

The Japanese occupation and later demolition reduced the seven wings to three, and independent India made the jail a national memorial in 1979. The museum tells the inmates' stories with restraint and power. Stay for the evening light-and-sound show, when the saga of sacrifice is narrated against the very walls that witnessed it - few historic sites in India move visitors quite like this one.

name: Sanchi Stupa
story:
On a quiet hill in Madhya Pradesh stands the Great Stupa of Sanchi, begun by the emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE to enshrine relics of the Buddha - the same Ashoka who, horrified by the slaughter of his Kalinga war, embraced Buddhism and spread it across Asia. The stone dome you see today, doubled in size under later rulers, is among the oldest stone monuments in India.

Sanchi's glory is its four toranas, carved gateways added around the 1st century BCE, whose panels retell the Buddha's life and Jataka tales in teeming detail - remarkably, the Buddha himself is shown only through symbols: a wheel, a tree, footprints, an empty throne. The site slept forgotten for centuries until its rediscovery in 1818 and careful restoration. Go in the soft light of morning; the hilltop silence is part of the teaching.

name: Kandariya Mahadeva Temple
story:
The Chandela kings raised some eighty-five temples at their capital of Khajuraho between the 10th and 12th centuries; about twenty-five survive, and Kandariya Mahadeva, built around 1025-1050 under King Vidyadhara, is the grandest. Its mountain-peak shikhara soars about 31 metres, ringed by hundreds of sculpted figures - gods, dancers, musicians, lovers - each barely three feet tall and carved with astonishing life.

The famous erotic panels are only a small fraction of the whole, woven into a larger celebration of every aspect of existence; scholars still debate their meaning, from tantric symbolism to reminders that desire must be left outside the sanctum. However you read them, the craftsmanship humbles. Visit the western group at sunrise, when the sandstone warms and the temples stand in rose-tinted silence before the crowds arrive.

name: Varanasi Ghats
story:
Varanasi is one of the oldest living cities on earth, and its soul lies along the eighty-odd ghats that step down to the Ganges. Hindus believe the river here flows toward Shiva, and that to die in Kashi is to be freed from the cycle of rebirth - so the ghats hold the whole of life and death in plain view: bathers at dawn, priests, pilgrims, wrestlers, silk-sellers, and the eternal pyres of Manikarnika, where cremation fires have burned without pause for centuries.

Take a boat at first light from Assi Ghat and drift north as the city wakes - temples, palaces and washermen all gilded by sunrise. Return at dusk to Dashashwamedh Ghat for the Ganga Aarti, when rows of young priests raise fire to the river in synchrony, bells ringing across the water. It is overwhelming, tender and utterly unmissable.

name: Kashi Vishwanath Temple
story:
The Kashi Vishwanath Temple enshrines one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, Shiva as Lord of the Universe, and for centuries it has been the pole star of Hindu pilgrimage - the heart of the city that many consider Hinduism's holiest. The temple has been destroyed and rebuilt repeatedly through history; the present shrine was raised in 1780 by the Maratha queen Ahilyabai Holkar, and Maharaja Ranjit Singh later gilded its spires with gold.

The narrow lanes of the old city funnel pilgrims towards darshan in a current of marigolds, milk and faith - non-Hindus can absorb the atmosphere from the surrounding bazaar, where sweets, silk and sacred ash change hands as they have for generations. The new Kashi Vishwanath Corridor, opened in 2021, links the temple directly to the river ghats, easing an ancient pilgrimage route.

name: Har Ki Pauri
story:
At Har Ki Pauri, the 'steps of the Lord', the Ganges completes her descent from the Himalaya and enters the plains of India - and for two thousand years and more, pilgrims have gathered at this ghat to touch the river where it is believed a footprint of Vishnu is impressed on stone. Haridwar is one of the seven holiest cities of Hinduism, and one of the four sites of the Kumbh Mela, the largest peaceful gathering on earth, held here every twelve years.

Each evening at dusk the Ganga Aarti transforms the ghat: priests swing great tiered lamps in unison, bells and chants roll across the water, and thousands of leaf-boats bearing flowers and flames are set afloat on the darkening river. Arrive early for a seat on the steps, and keep a respectful distance from the powerful current.

name: Badrinath Temple
story:
High in the Garhwal Himalaya at about 3,100 metres, between the peaks named Nar and Narayan, stands Badrinath, one of the four Char Dham and among the most revered of Vishnu's shrines. Tradition holds that the philosopher Adi Shankaracharya established the temple in the 8th century, recovering the deity's black stone image from the icy Alaknanda river that thunders past the town.

Snow closes the shrine for half the year; when the doors open around late April or May, hundreds of thousands make the mountain journey before winter returns in November. Before darshan, pilgrims bathe in the Tapt Kund, a natural hot spring steaming beside the freezing river - one of the strangest and most welcome sensations in Himalayan travel. The rainbow-painted facade against snow peaks is a sight that justifies every hairpin bend.

name: Kedarnath Temple
story:
At 3,583 metres, ringed by snow peaks near the source of the Mandakini, Kedarnath is the highest and among the holiest of the twelve Jyotirlingas. Legend says the Pandava brothers sought Shiva here after the great war of the Mahabharata, and that he eluded them as a bull, sinking into the earth and leaving his hump behind as the linga. Adi Shankaracharya is traditionally credited with establishing the shrine in the 8th century.

The temple stands open only from late spring to autumn; pilgrims trek some sixteen kilometres up from Gaurikund, a route of waterfalls, ponies and extraordinary resolve. In the catastrophic floods of June 2013 the valley was devastated, yet the temple survived - a massive boulder lodged behind it and split the torrent, an event many still speak of with awe. Book ahead, acclimatise, and walk slowly; the mountain sets the terms.

name: Vaishno Devi Temple
story:
In the Trikuta hills above the town of Katra, a cave shrine houses the goddess Vaishno Devi, worshipped as three natural rock forms - pindis - representing Maha Kali, Maha Lakshmi and Maha Saraswati. By tradition the goddess meditated in these mountains, and legend tells how she vanquished the demon Bhairon Nath, who in repentance received her blessing; his shrine near the summit completes the pilgrimage.

It is among the most visited shrines in all of India, drawing many millions each year. The thirteen-kilometre climb from Katra, paved and lit, moves to the chant of Jai Mata Di as families, elderly pilgrims and entire villages walk together through the night. The moment inside the cave, when you stoop past the three sacred stones in the dim lamplight, repays every step.

name: Rumtek Monastery
story:
Across the valley from Gangtok, Rumtek is the seat in exile of the Karmapa, head of the Karma Kagyu lineage of Tibetan Buddhism. When the 16th Karmapa fled Tibet in 1959, Sikkim gave him this hilltop, and through the 1960s monks rebuilt their monastery as a faithful echo of Tsurphu, the order's ancient seat in Tibet - its great shrine hall rose as a vessel for a tradition carried over the mountains.

The main hall glows with murals, silk banners and a towering golden stupa holding relics of the 16th Karmapa; in the adjacent institute, young monks debate Buddhist philosophy with theatrical hand-claps. Time a visit for the masked Cham dances before Losar, the Tibetan New Year, when the courtyard fills with swirling brocade and long horns - a fragment of old Tibet living on a Sikkimese ridge.

name: Tsomgo Lake
story:
At about 3,750 metres on the old trade route towards Nathu La and Tibet, Tsomgo - the Changu lake - is a glacial tarn held sacred by the Sikkimese; Buddhist monks once studied its changing colours to read the seasons ahead. The lake stays frozen through winter, then melts into a shoreline loud with primulas and rhododendrons by late spring.

The road from Gangtok climbs about forty kilometres through waterfalls and army posts, and the lake appears suddenly, steel-blue beneath the peaks, with yaks waiting placidly for riders along its bank. Permits are required and arranged through local operators; foreign visitors have some restrictions, so check ahead. Go early before clouds build, sip hot tea at the stalls, and let the thin mountain air slow you down.

name: Living Root Bridges
story:
In the rain-drenched Khasi hills of Meghalaya, around villages near Cherrapunji and Nongriat, people do not build bridges - they grow them. For generations, villagers have guided the aerial roots of rubber fig trees across rivers, training them over years until the roots knit into living spans strong enough to bear dozens of people. A bridge may take decades to mature, but it can serve for centuries, growing stronger as the tree lives.

The most famous is the double-decker root bridge at Nongriat, reached by descending several thousand steps into the gorge - a walk through betel groves, butterflies and waterfalls in one of the wettest landscapes on earth. Go slowly, hire a village guide, and remember you are walking on something no engineer made: patience itself, given form.

name: Kaziranga National Park
story:
Kaziranga's floodplains on the Brahmaputra hold two-thirds of the world's greater one-horned rhinoceroses - an animal brought back here from the edge of extinction. The park's founding story is beloved: in 1904, Lady Curzon, wife of the Viceroy, visited hoping to see a rhino and found none; her questions helped spur protection, and the reserve was established soon after, in 1905.

A century of conservation made Kaziranga a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Asia's great wildlife spectacles: tall elephant grass hiding rhinos, wild buffalo, swamp deer and one of the highest densities of tigers recorded anywhere, with elephants moving through in herds. Safari jeeps run in the early morning and afternoon from Kohora; visit between November and April, as monsoon floods close the park - floods the grassland, remarkably, needs to survive.

name: Alappuzha Backwaters
story:
Lord Curzon is said to have called Alappuzha the Venice of the East, and the comparison understates it: behind this old spice-port town lies a vast waterworld of canals, lagoons and rice paddies at or below sea level, where ferries, canoes and schoolchildren all travel by water. The British-era port has faded, but the backwaters made Alappuzha the heart of Kerala's houseboat country.

The kettuvallams - great rice barges of jackwood and coir, once used to haul grain - have been reborn as houseboats; an overnight cruise through Vembanad lake, past toddy tappers and kingfishers, is one of India's essential journeys. On the second Saturday of August, the Nehru Trophy Boat Race fills Punnamada lake with hundred-foot snake boats rowed by a hundred chanting oarsmen - a spectacle born when Nehru visited in 1952 and, thrilled, donated a trophy.

name: Chinese Fishing Nets
story:
Along the Fort Kochi shore, giant cantilevered nets dip and rise against the harbour mouth - the Chinese fishing nets, by far the most photographed sight in Kochi. Local tradition credits traders from the court of Kublai Khan with introducing them around the 14th century, and they remain unlike anything else in India: shore-operated contraptions of teak and bamboo, counterweighted by stones, needing a team of men to work.

Come at sunset, when the nets silhouette against the molten sky and fishermen pull up the day's modest catch. You can buy fish straight off the nets and have it grilled at the stalls behind - about as fresh as seafood gets. Walk on to the nearby St. Francis Church and the lanes of old Fort Kochi, where four centuries of Portuguese, Dutch and British India still show in every gable.

name: St. Francis Church
story:
Built in 1503 by Portuguese Franciscan friars, St. Francis Church is the oldest European church in India - a plain, gabled building whose quiet interior holds one of history's great footnotes: Vasco da Gama, who opened the sea route from Europe to India, died in Kochi in 1524 and was first buried here, before his remains were later taken home to Portugal. His gravestone still marks the spot.

The church changed hands with the town: Catholic under the Portuguese, Protestant under the Dutch, Anglican under the British, and today a church of the Church of South India. Its hand-operated punkah fans and old Dutch gravestones conjure centuries of colonial Sundays. Combine it with the nearby Santa Cruz Basilica and the Chinese fishing nets for a perfect Fort Kochi morning.

name: Padmanabhaswamy Temple
story:
Kerala's capital is named for its god: Thiruvananthapuram, the city of the sacred serpent Ananta, on whom Vishnu reclines in eternal yogic sleep within this temple. The great idol, seen through three doors - face, navel with Brahma on a lotus, and feet - is among the most awe-inspiring images in Indian worship. The temple was magnificently rebuilt in the 18th century by Marthanda Varma, who did something no other king had done: he surrendered his kingdom to the deity, ruling thereafter as Padmanabha's servant - a title Travancore's royals still hold.

The shrine's guarded vaults made headlines in 2011 when inventories revealed treasure of almost unimaginable value, accumulated over centuries of royal offering. Entry requires traditional dress - dhoti for men, saree or dhoti for women - and is restricted to Hindus; all can admire the seven-storey gopuram from the Padmatheertham tank across the road.

name: Bekal Fort
story:
Bekal is the largest fort in Kerala, a great keyhole-shaped citadel of laterite stone that thrusts its walls straight into the Arabian Sea. It rose in the 17th century under the Nayakas of Keladi, passed through the hands of the Kolathiri rajas, Mysore's Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan, and finally the British - yet its design was purely defensive: no palace ever stood here, only bastions, magazines and a watchtower with a sea view that now thrills photographers.

A walkway along the ramparts gives a panorama of surf, beach and coconut groves that film directors discovered long ago. Below the sea wall, waves burst through rock channels at high tide. Come late in the afternoon, walk the full circuit, and stay for sunset over the water - one of the finest on the Malabar coast.

name: Jatayu Earth's Center
story:
High on a rocky hill in Kerala's Kollam district sprawls the world's largest bird sculpture: Jatayu, the noble vulture of the Ramayana, two hundred feet from wingtip to wingtip. Legend says it was on this very rock that Jatayu fell, mortally wounded after battling Ravana to stop the abduction of Sita - his dying words to Rama pointed the way to Lanka.

Sculptor-filmmaker Rajiv Anchal spent years realising the monument, which opened in 2018 as the centrepiece of a nature and adventure park: a cable car climbs the hill, and the giant bird itself houses a museum and a 6D theatre. Even skeptics admit the sculpture is stupendous against the green hills. Combine it with a stop at nearby backwaters or make it a day trip from Thiruvananthapuram or Kollam.

name: Munnar
story:
Munnar means three rivers, and the town sits where three mountain streams meet at around 1,600 metres in Kerala's Western Ghats. British planters of the 19th century found its cool heights perfect for tea, and the hills remain draped in tea gardens to this day - an unbroken geometry of green that makes Munnar one of South India's most loved escapes.

Walk or cycle the estate lanes, visit a working tea factory to see leaf become brew, and climb towards Top Station for views into the plains of Tamil Nadu. Nearby Eravikulam National Park protects the endangered Nilgiri tahr on grassy peaks, and once every twelve years the hillsides turn blue-purple with the mass flowering of the neelakurinji. Mornings are for mist; carry a light jacket and a flask, and let the mountains pour the tea.

name: Abbey Falls
story:
A short drive from Madikeri, the capital of Kodagu, the young Kaveri river drops about seventy feet through a gorge of coffee bushes and spice trees at Abbey Falls - one of Coorg's signature sights. A hanging bridge faces the cascade, and in and after the monsoon the falls roar white through the green, filling the air with spray.

The walk down from the car park passes private coffee estates heavy with pepper vines and cardamom - Kodagu grows much of India's coffee, and the Kodava people who farm it have a proud martial culture of their own. Pair the falls with sunset at Raja's Seat in Madikeri, the garden where Kodagu's kings once watched the sun sink over the western hills, and you have Coorg's classic day.

name: Raja's Seat
story:
Raja's Seat is a modest garden with a royal past: the kings of Kodagu are said to have spent their evenings on this Madikeri ridge, watching the sun drop into valleys that roll westward towards Kerala. The view remains the point - layer after layer of blue-green hills, with mist pooling in the folds at dusk.

Come around sunrise or sunset, when the valleys fill with light and cloud in turn. The garden itself, with its flowers, toy train and an old pavilion, is pleasantly old-fashioned; locals promenade here as they have for generations. It takes less than an hour, costs little, and delivers the essence of Coorg - highland air, distance, and the slow theatre of a mountain evening.

name: Cubbon Park
story:
Cubbon Park is the green heart of Bengaluru: some three hundred acres of bamboo groves, fig trees and shaded avenues laid out in 1870 by Richard Sankey, chief engineer of Mysore, and named for Mark Cubbon, the longest-serving British commissioner of the kingdom. What began as a hundred acres grew as successive administrators added land, and today it is where the city comes to breathe.

Ringed by Vidhana Soudha's granite grandeur and the rose-red High Court building of 1868, the Attara Kacheri, the park shelters joggers at dawn, chess players under the rain trees, and the lovely red State Central Library at its core. Sunday mornings, when traffic is barred, show Bengaluru at its gentlest - bring coffee from a nearby darshini and claim a bench under a century-old tree.

name: Lalbagh Botanical Garden
story:
Lalbagh began in 1760 as a private royal garden laid out by Hyder Ali, ruler of Mysore, and was enriched by his son Tipu Sultan with trees and plants gathered from as far as Persia, Afghanistan and Mauritius. Later British superintendents made it one of the great botanical gardens of the tropics - 240 acres holding species collected across two and a half centuries.

The cast-iron Glass House, raised in 1889 on the model of London's Crystal Palace, hosts the famous Republic Day and Independence Day flower shows. But Lalbagh's oldest resident is stone: the Lalbagh Rock, a peninsular gneiss outcrop around three billion years old, among the oldest rocks on earth, crowned by a watchtower from Kempegowda's era. Come at opening time, when walkers and birds have the garden to themselves.

name: Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace
story:
In the heart of old Bengaluru, near the city market, stands the teakwood pleasure palace of Tipu Sultan, the Tiger of Mysore. Begun by his father Hyder Ali within the old fort and completed around 1791, it carried the proud inscription Rash-e-Jannat - envy of heaven. From its painted balconies Tipu held durbar during the fierce years when Mysore alone in southern India stood against the East India Company.

The palace is small but exquisite: every pillar, arch and ceiling of dark teak was once covered in floral paint, traces of which survive. Tipu died defending Srirangapatna in 1799, and the British used this very palace as their secretariat. The small museum inside displays his portraits and memorabilia - an intimate window on one of India's most formidable rulers.

name: Bangalore Palace
story:
Bangalore Palace looks like it wandered out of England: fortified towers, turrets and battlements in Tudor and Scottish-baronial style, inspired, it is often said, by Windsor Castle. The property began as a school principal's house and was bought in the 1870s for the young Maharaja of Mysore, Chamarajendra Wadiyar, whose family expanded it into the fantasy of gables and gardens you see today.

Inside, the audio tour winds past ballroom, durbar hall and hunting trophies - the maharaja's courtly life preserved in teak, stained glass and family photographs. The palace grounds now host rock concerts beneath the turrets, a happily un-Tudor fate. It is one of the few great Indian palaces still owned by its royal family, and their affection for the place shows in every corner.
